title: Haematemesis in a man with cirrhosis
presentation: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought in after two large-volume episodes of haematemesis and black stools since this morning. Triage: HR 118, BP 92/58, RR 20, SpO2 96% on air, T 36.8 C. He is pale and slightly drowsy.

stages.label: History
stages.text: Cirrhosis diagnosed three years ago; Child-Pugh B at clinic four months ago. Endoscopy 18 months ago showed small oesophageal varices with no red signs; he was started on propranolol but stopped it 'because it made me tired'. Ascites controlled on spironolactone and furosemide. He drank six to eight beers a day until a week ago, when he stopped because of a sore shoulder, for which he has taken ibuprofen 400 mg three or four times a day for two weeks. No previous bleeds. No anticoagulants or antiplatelets. No known hepatic encephalopathy. No retching before the first haematemesis. No chest pain.
stages.prompt: What are the likely sources of this bleed, and what do you do in the first 15 minutes, before you know which it is?
stages.learner_goal: Keep both variceal and NSAID-related peptic bleeding on the list, and start resuscitation and empirical cirrhosis-specific therapy without waiting for endoscopy.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: HR 114, BP 94/60, cool peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds. Oriented to person and place but not time; mild asterixis. Jaundiced, spider naevi, palmar erythema, moderate ascites, splenomegaly. Melaena on rectal examination. No further haematemesis in the department so far. Chest clear. Airway patent with an intact gag reflex; he is protecting his airway.
stages.prompt: Set your transfusion targets and tell me what else you are giving him now. When does he get his endoscopy, and what has to happen first?
stages.learner_goal: Apply a restrictive transfusion threshold, give a vasoactive drug and antibiotics, consider the airway, and plan endoscopy within 12 hours once resuscitated.

available_tests.chemistry: Na 131, K 4.1, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), BUN 48, bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, ALT 48, AST 96, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, glucose 110.
available_tests.group and crossmatch: Blood group O positive, antibody screen negative; four units of packed red cells crossmatched.
available_tests.ascitic tap: Diagnostic paracentesis: WBC 120 per microlitre, neutrophils 40 per microlitre, protein 1.1 g/dL. No spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
available_tests.chest x-ray: Clear lung fields, no free air under the diaphragm, normal heart size.

stages.label: Resuscitation and endoscopy
stages.text: Two large-bore cannulas are placed. He receives 500 mL of crystalloid, two units of packed red cells (Hb 8.1 after the second), an octreotide bolus and infusion, intravenous ceftriaxone, and erythromycin 30 minutes before the scope. He is not intubated; he stays alert enough to protect his airway. Endoscopy at eight hours: three columns of large oesophageal varices with red wale marks and active oozing from one column in the distal oesophagus, treated with five bands with haemostasis. A 6 mm clean-based ulcer in the antrum (Forrest III), not bleeding. No gastric varices; no bleeding from portal hypertensive gastropathy. Post-procedure HR 96, BP 110/70.
stages.prompt: Commit to the diagnosis. Lay out the next five days: which drugs continue and for how long, what are you watching for, and what stops this happening again?
stages.learner_goal: Name acute variceal haemorrhage, continue octreotide and antibiotics for the right duration, prevent encephalopathy and withdrawal, and set up secondary prophylaxis.

diagnosis: Acute oesophageal variceal haemorrhage in alcohol-related cirrhosis (with an incidental, non-bleeding NSAID-associated antral ulcer)
key_clues: Known cirrhosis with documented varices and a discontinued beta-blocker
Large-volume haematemesis with shock, splenomegaly and ascites (portal hypertension)
Haemoglobin fall from 11 to 7.2 with a disproportionately raised BUN
Endoscopy: large varices with red wale marks and active oozing, treated with band ligation
Clean-based antral ulcer (Forrest III) without stigmata of recent bleeding

distractors.name: NSAID-related peptic ulcer bleed
distractors.why_not: An antral ulcer is present and the ibuprofen made this a genuine possibility, but the ulcer has a clean base with no stigmata while a varix was actively oozing. Both had to be covered until the scope, which is why a PPI before endoscopy is also reasonable.

distractors.name: Mallory-Weiss tear
distractors.why_not: No retching before the first haematemesis, the bleed caused shock, and no tear was seen.

distractors.name: Portal hypertensive gastropathy
distractors.why_not: Causes slow oozing and chronic anaemia rather than haemodynamic collapse, and was not bleeding at endoscopy.

distractors.name: Gastric varices
distractors.why_not: None seen; they would have required cyanoacrylate injection or early TIPS rather than banding.

distractors.name: Bleeding driven by coagulopathy
distractors.why_not: INR 1.9 reflects reduced synthesis of both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors and does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis; FFP adds volume and portal pressure and is not indicated to 'correct' it.

distractors.name: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis as the precipitant
distractors.why_not: Ascitic neutrophil count is 40; antibiotics are given anyway, because bacterial infection is present in up to half of cirrhotic bleeders and prophylaxis reduces rebleeding and death.

rubric.description: Differential includes both variceal bleeding and an NSAID-related peptic source
rubric.concept: About a third of upper GI bleeds in cirrhosis are non-variceal; keep the peptic branch open until endoscopy

rubric.description: Secures two large-bore lines and crossmatches blood in the first minutes
rubric.concept: Resuscitation starts before diagnosis: access, crossmatch, early blood

rubric.description: Uses a restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb about 7, target 7-9) and explains that over-transfusion raises portal pressure
rubric.concept: Restrictive transfusion (threshold 7 g/dL) improves survival in cirrhotic upper GI bleeding

rubric.description: Starts octreotide (or terlipressin) empirically before endoscopy
rubric.concept: Vasoactive therapy for suspected variceal bleeding starts on suspicion, not on endoscopic confirmation
Antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhotic GI bleeding reduces infection, rebleeding and mortality

rubric.description: Plans endoscopy within 12 hours once haemodynamically resuscitated
rubric.concept: Endoscopy within 12 hours of presentation for suspected variceal bleeding, after resuscitation

rubric.description: Considers airway protection given confusion and ongoing haematemesis
rubric.concept: Encephalopathy plus haematemesis is an aspiration risk; intubate for endoscopy if the airway is not protected

rubric.description: Sets up secondary prophylaxis: non-selective beta-blocker plus a banding programme (or TIPS in high-risk patients)
rubric.concept: NSBB plus endoscopic band ligation is standard secondary prophylaxis after variceal bleeding

management_summary: Acute variceal bleed, now banded. Continue octreotide 50 micrograms/h for two to five days and ceftriaxone 1 g daily for seven days. Restrictive transfusion: target Hb 7 to 8 g/dL; do not give FFP to 'fix' the INR, and give platelets only for active bleeding with a count under 50. Lactulose to two or three soft stools a day to prevent encephalopathy from the blood load; thiamine, folate and a symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocol for alcohol withdrawal (last drink a week ago, but watch). Hold the diuretics until haemodynamically stable and renal function recovers, and monitor for acute kidney injury and infection. Short course of pantoprazole for the antral ulcer and post-banding ulcers; stop ibuprofen for good. Secondary prophylaxis before discharge: carvedilol (or propranolol) titrated to heart rate 55 to 60 with systolic over 90, plus repeat banding every two to four weeks until eradicated, then surveillance. Child-Pugh C, or B with active bleeding at endoscopy, qualifies for discussion of pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours; refer to hepatology and alcohol services.
teaching_points: In a cirrhotic with haematemesis, treat for varices before the scope: a vasoactive drug (octreotide or terlipressin) and antibiotic prophylaxis each independently reduce rebleeding and mortality, and the diagnosis is confirmed only at endoscopy, within 12 hours once resuscitated.

Transfuse at a haemoglobin of 7 (target 7 to 9): the Villanueva trial showed a restrictive strategy improved survival, largely in Child A and B cirrhosis, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding. The INR in cirrhosis is not a bleeding risk; FFP is not a corrective.

A cirrhotic can still have a peptic ulcer, especially on NSAIDs; about a third of upper GI bleeds in cirrhosis are non-variceal. Keep the peptic branch open until endoscopy, and give a PPI if there is any ulcer.

A bleed is a decompensating event. Prevent the next crises: lactulose for encephalopathy, watch for withdrawal, infection and AKI, start a non-selective beta-blocker plus a banding programme, and consider early TIPS in high-risk patients.
references: Garcia-Tsao G et al. Portal hypertensive bleeding in cirrhosis: risk stratification, diagnosis, and management: 2016 practice guidance by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatology 2017;65:310-35
Villanueva C et al. Transfusion strategies for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. N Engl J Med 2013;368:11-21
de Franchis R et al. Baveno VII - Renewing consensus in portal hypertension. J Hepatol 2022;76:959-74
